newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Europe links key to French aerospace - Jospin.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Europe links key to French aerospace - Jospin.

text.p: Newly-elected Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin pledged financial support for the French aerospace industry on Saturday but stressed that European cooperation would be essential to keep costs down.

French and European companies are eyeing the current round of U.S. mega-mergers with concern as their sources of funding are too narrow to keep up with soaring programme costs and competition is increasing rapidly in the world market.
"The government will give support to French companies," Jospin said in a speech to the Paris air show.

"It will notably do so, within international accords, by granting not only research funds but also repayable launch aid to allow the sharing of risks associated with development of new products before they come to market," he said.

He added: "This effort must today be conducted within a European framework from the first phases. No future programme, whether it be civil or military, can from now escape the imperative of cooperation".

Jospin called for greater efforts to cut costs in military projects and said the government needed to improve its procurement process by moving towards a system of multi-year funding for high priority programmes.
Under current rules, the National Assembly votes procurement funds annually, keeping production batches short and driving up manufacturers' costs. Companies have long called for a reform.

France has the resources to be a full part of a more integrated European aerospace and defence industry, he said. "The government is determined to favour this evolution, on the base of defined industrial projects," Jospin said.

Private firms British Aerospace Plc and Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG of Germany are eager to build an integrated European civil and military industry to face up to the U.S. threat, but feel France is dragging its feet by keeping national company Aerospatiale in state control.

A vital part of that consolidation lies in changing the Airbus Industrie consortium into a limited company, where a disagreement over control of Airbus assets has put Aerospatiale at odds with its partners.
"I know the (Airbus) negotiations are difficult. They will not be successful if we do not take into account the skills and capabilities of each of its partners," Jospin said.

Jospin also said he was "very worried" about exclusive supply agreements between U.S. aircraft giant Boeing Co and American Airlines, Continental and Delta, saying that competition should be fair and open. These deals exclude Airbus from these airlines for more than 20 years.

Jospin gave little away on the issues at the forefront of industrial consolidation -- the government's plans for defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF and a planned merger of Aerospatiale and combat plane maker Dassault Aviation.
A merger of Dassault and Aerospatiale, followed by a privatisation of the new group, was a key plank in the defence industry shake-out planned by the previous government.
"Already, I can indicate to you that I consider it essential to bring together the civil and military capabilities in the aeronautical sector," Jospin said.
National interest will be the "sole measure" on deciding Thomson-CSF's future and the government will not rule out any options in developing the company, he said.

The conservative government last year launched the sale of the state's 58 percent stake in Thomson-CSF but lost power three weeks ago to the Socialists, whose election campaign was hostile to privatisations.
